newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa weathers the emerging markets storm.
newsitem.headline: South Africa weathers the emerging markets storm.

text.p: Emerging market currency turmoil and a meltdown in gold prices to 12-year lows over recent weeks has stoked concerns among some investors about possible renewed pressure on the rand.
Foreigners have turned wary of South African bonds, chalking up net sales of 1.005 billion rand ($220.7 million) in the past three days.

But analysts said on Thursday South Africa's structural differences with many other emerging markets, notably its relatively modest current account deficit, should shield the local unit for the time being.
In addition, many believe the rand took its medicine last year when it shed more than a fifth of its value on a trade-weighted basis following fierce speculative attacks.

"The problems that the other emerging markets had were specifically related to large uncovered dollar positions in the corporate sector, an overvalued currency and the fact that they had huge current account deficits," said SBC Warburg economist Michael McClintock.
These factors do not apply in South Africa, he said.
At the same time the central Reserve Bank has proved more successful this year than last at managing the currency, capping the unit in recent days below 4.56 to the dollar, analysts added.

Thailand, weighed down by a massive current accounts deficit, implemented an effective devaluation of the baht earlier this month, while the Philippines last week allowed similar measures for its peso.
This week attention has shifted to possible devaluation in Brazil, although the authorities have denied any plans to shift forex policy.
The rand, meanwhile, has charted a comparatively orderly depreciation in July of less than four percent against the dollar after holding remarkably steady in the first half of the year.

CS First Boston senior international economist Shawn Shetley noted the emerging market currencies which had suffered most of late were labouring under current account deficits running at over five percent of GDP.
By comparison, South Africa carried a first quarter shortfall representing just 1.4 percent of GDP.
South Africa's markets have also nervously eyed gold's fall, viewing it as a possible threat to the current account.
But central bank governor Chris Stals echoed analyst opinion that, at least at the current prices, the gold meltdown should not create any undue pressure on the balance of payments.

"Should the present price of $320 (an ounce) be maintained for a full year, the loss in foreign exchange on the balance of payments will amount to 4.5 billion rand, or less than three percent of total exports," he told a business lunch on Wednesday.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Gordon Smith noted: "As the gold price has declined so the terms of trade have deteriorated but that has been hedged by the decline in the oil price.
"The overall current account exposure in terms of the direction of the terms of trade today is actually still better than in January."

Also working in the rand's favour was the fact that there had been no flight of capital following the relaxation of foreign exchange controls on July 1, which allowed individuals to invest offshore for the first time.
Analysts said the trade-weighted rand was currently close to equilibrium.
"On a trade-weighted basis the currency is at exactly fair value and beginning to move into overvalued territory," said Deutsche's Smith.
SBC's McClintock added: "If there aren't specific economic fundamentals pointing to a de-equilibrium in the currency, the speculators probably won't be able to move it the way they did in Asia."
-- Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003 ($ = 4.554 South African Rand)
